hints: Focus on what the charge tells you, a positive charge means electrons lost and a negative charge means electrons gained.
Start by writing down the atomic number (proton number) for B, Be, H and He, then adjust for the 3+, 2+, 1- and 1+ charges.
Count the final electrons for each species and look for the one that is left with only a single electron.
walkthrough:
**Recall How To Count Electrons In Ions**

For a neutral atom, electrons equals protons equals atomic number. For an ion, adjust for the charge.

$$\text{electrons in ion} = \text{atomic number} - \text{ionic charge}$$

**Calculate Electrons For Each Species**

Let us work through them one by one, it is quick and simple.

$$\text{B}^{3+}: 5 - (+3) = 2 \text{ electrons}$$
$$\text{Be}^{2+}: 4 - (+2) = 2 \text{ electrons}$$
$$\text{H}^{-}: 1 - (-1) = 1 + 1 = 2 \text{ electrons}$$
$$\text{He}^{+}: 2 - (+1) = 1 \text{ electron}$$

**Compare And Pick The Smallest**

Three of the species are isoelectronic with helium, they all have 2 electrons. Only one species has fewer than that, with just 1 electron left.

That species contains the smallest number of electrons.

options.A: Boron has atomic number 5, so $\text{B}^{3+}$ has $5 - 3 = 2$ electrons. This is the same as a helium atom, not the smallest.
options.B: Beryllium has atomic number 4, so $\text{Be}^{2+}$ has $4 - 2 = 2$ electrons. This ties with two other options, so it is not the smallest.
options.C: Hydrogen has atomic number 1, so $\text{H}^{-}$ gains one electron to give $1 + 1 = 2$ electrons. Students sometimes think H- has only 1 electron, but the minus means one extra electron.
options.D: Helium has atomic number 2, so $\text{He}^{+}$ has $2 - 1 = 1$ electron. This is fewer than the 2 electrons in all the other species, so it is the smallest.
